analysis.title: Market Insights Weekly, 6 November 2026
key_insights: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 25bp to 4.00% on Thursday, its first hike in more than three years. The hike was expected, but the outlook was more hawkish than expected.
The MPC vote was 8-1 for a 25bp hike, with Catherine Mann preferring 50bp. Even the most dovish members, Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor, voted for a hike.

The BoE now forecasts CPI at 4.4% in Q1 2027 and a peak of 4.9% in Q2. The driver is a larger and more persistent global energy shock. The forecast assumes Brent above $115/barrel this quarter. Resilient growth and a stabilising labour market raise the risk of inflation broadening beyond energy.

Governor Bailey said a second hike is 'probably more likely than not' but pushed back against a long sequence of increases. Money markets price a slightly above-evens chance of another rise in December.

Democrats won both the House and Senate in the US midterms. This constrains President Trump's domestic agenda and gives Democrats more influence over legislation, spending, appointments and oversight. They lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override a veto, and Trump keeps considerable executive authority over foreign policy.

Market reaction to the midterms differed by asset class. US equities first rallied on expected gridlock, then technology stocks fell on concern that Democratic control could bring more scrutiny of AI expansion.

Brent fell as low as $93/barrel, below $100 for the first time since early October, as markets speculated about pressure to de-escalate the Middle East conflict. VP Vance linked the Republican defeat to the war, and a Democratic Congress could use spending powers to constrain funding. The implications remain highly uncertain because the President keeps foreign policy latitude.
The oil decline came too late for the BoE projections and would not have changed the decision. If sustained, lower energy prices would ease some of the inflation pressure in the BoE forecast.

Lloyds expects UK GDP of +0.1% m/m in September and +0.8% q/q in Q3, the strongest quarter since early 2022 and above the BoE's 0.7% estimate. Consumer spending and AI investment supported growth. Higher energy prices, tighter financial conditions and weaker October GfK consumer confidence point to softer growth ahead. The Lloyds Business Barometer rose 6 points to 47%.
US October nonfarm payrolls rose 165k, with prior months revised higher, and unemployment fell to 4.1% despite higher participation. This gives the Fed scope to keep focusing on inflation.
Lloyds expects October US CPI at 0.2% m/m headline and 0.2% m/m core, versus consensus of 0.3% headline and 0.2% core. An upside surprise would reinforce expectations of another Fed hike in December.

September US CPI rose 0.6% m/m (3.7% y/y, from 3.4%), driven by gasoline, and core rose 0.3% m/m (2.6% y/y). October 2025 CPI is unavailable because of the government shutdown late last year, so the matching y/y rates will not be published.

Reflects a larger and more persistent global energy shock and risk of broadening inflation, supporting a more hawkish BoE outlook.
The BoE inflation projection assumes this level. Actual prices fell well below it after the midterms.
First move below $100 since early October on speculation of Middle East de-escalation. Lower prices would reduce inflation pressure if sustained.
Robust jobs growth with upward revisions to prior months shows the economy absorbing higher rates and gives the Fed room to focus on inflation.
Fell despite higher participation, which signals labour market resilience.
The strongest monthly increase since the early part of the Middle East war, driven by gasoline prices.
Up from 3.4% on higher energy prices.
Lloyds expects a sharp moderation on lower gasoline prices. Consensus is 0.3%. An upside surprise would raise expectations of a December Fed hike.
Consensus is also 0.2%. Core is the focus for policymakers.
Would be the strongest quarter since Q1 2022, above the BoE's 0.7% estimate and consensus of 0.7%.
Consensus is 0.0%. Services, industrial production and construction are all forecast to contribute positively.
Left the economy on course for another solid quarterly expansion.
Rose 6 points, so business confidence held up better than consumer confidence.

risk_factors: Higher energy prices erode UK household purchasing power and raise business costs, and tighter financial conditions add a headwind to growth.
Inflation could broaden beyond energy given resilient growth and a stabilising labour market.
Democratic scrutiny of AI expansion is a risk for technology stocks.
The Middle East policy outlook is highly uncertain because the President keeps latitude over foreign policy.
An upside surprise in October US CPI would raise expectations of another Fed hike in December.
vol_and_positioning: Money markets price a slightly above-evens chance of another BoE hike in December.
Lloyds says an upside US CPI surprise would reinforce expectations for another Fed rate rise in December.
geopolitical: US midterm elections: Democrats took control of the House and Senate, defeating President Trump's Republicans.

Middle East conflict: markets speculate the Republican defeat could increase pressure on the administration to de-escalate. VP Vance linked the defeat to the war, and a Democratic Congress could constrain funding through its spending powers. The President retains significant latitude over foreign policy.
Global energy shock: a larger and more persistent shock is driving the BoE's higher inflation forecasts.

tension_points.bull_case: Governor Bailey said a second hike is 'probably more likely than not', and money markets price a slightly above-evens chance of a December rise. Inflation is forecast to peak at 4.9% in Q2 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: Bailey pushed back against a long sequence of increases, and the MPC is divided on what follows the unanimous vote. Lower oil prices could reduce the inflation pressure in the forecast.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A sustained fall in energy prices below the BoE's Brent assumption of above $115/barrel would reduce the inflation pressure built into its forecast.

tension_points.theme: US October CPI and Fed December hike
tension_points.bull_case: Resilient payrolls and unemployment at 4.1% give the Fed scope to focus on inflation, and an upside CPI surprise would reinforce expectations of a December hike.
tension_points.bear_case: Lloyds expects headline CPI of 0.2% m/m and core of 0.2%, helped by lower gasoline prices, which would ease hike expectations.
tension_points.what_invalidates: October US CPI above the 0.2% m/m Lloyds forecast (consensus 0.3% headline) would strengthen the case for a December hike.
